description: A perennial herb or subshrub 1-1.5 m tall with pinnate leaves of 9-17 ovate leaflets, spikes of pale blue to violet pea-like flowers and flat reddish-brown pods. The long, woody, yellow-brown taproot and runners have a distinctive sweet taste.
cultural_significance: Yashtimadhu is among the most widely used drugs in Ayurveda and appears in countless formulations. The word means 'sweet stick'. Mulethi sticks are chewed for sore throat and as a mouth freshener across India.
habitat: Subtropical to warm temperate dry regions with deep, sandy, well-drained soil; mostly imported or cultivated in India (Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal).

uses.title: Cough, sore throat and hoarse voice
uses.detail: Yashtimadhu is described as Kanthya (good for the throat and voice) and Kaphahara; it is sucked or taken in decoction.

uses.title: Acidity and gastric discomfort
uses.detail: Traditionally used in hyperacidity and ulcer-like conditions as a Pittahara; deglycyrrhizinated liquorice (DGL) is studied for stomach protection.

uses.title: Eye and skin care
uses.detail: The root is described as Chakshushya, Varnya and Keshya; used in eye washes and external applications.

uses.title: Wound healing and mouth ulcers
uses.detail: Powder with ghee or honey is traditionally applied to wounds and mouth ulcers (Vranaropana).

uses.title: Rasayana (rejuvenative)
uses.detail: Considered a Jivaniya and Balya drug used as a general tonic.

classical_refs: Charaka Samhita: listed among Jivaniya and Kanthya groups

preparations.name: Yashtimadhu churna
preparations.method: Dry the root and powder it.
preparations.note: Used in cough, acidity and throat formulations.

preparations.name: Yashtimadhu kwatha
preparations.method: Boil crushed root in water and strain.
preparations.note: Traditionally given for cough and acidity.

preparations.name: Mulethi stick
preparations.method: Chew or suck a small piece of root.
preparations.note: Household use for sore throat; limit use.

preparations.name: Yashtimadhu ghrita or taila
preparations.method: Medicated ghee or oil made with liquorice.
preparations.note: Used externally or internally under practitioner guidance.

precautions: Regular or high intake can raise blood pressure and lower potassium, cause water retention and swelling, and strain the heart; avoid in hypertension, heart or kidney disease and with diuretics, digoxin or corticosteroids. Avoid in pregnancy and long-term use. Deglycyrrhizinated forms are safer for the stomach.

cultivation.propagation: Rhizome or stolon cuttings in spring
cultivation.harvest: Roots harvested after 3-4 years in autumn

conservation_status: Not threatened globally; wild collection in some regions is heavy.
fun_fact: Glycyrrhizin is roughly 30-50 times sweeter than sugar by weight.
